newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan individual stock options seen starting slow.
newsitem.headline: Japan individual stock options seen starting slow.

text.p: Investors are looking forward to Friday's scheduled launch of individual stock option trading on Japan's bourses, but market sources say it may take time for trade to pick up.
"We are not going to measure success by the trading volume on July 18 or the few months after that," said David Heller, managing director of equities at Goldman Sachs.

"We view it as a first step in the process towards openness in the marketplace and towards introducing products which are going to be relevant for risk management and return enhancement," he said in a recent interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
Japan's experience in stock derivatives goes back to the late 1980s, when index futures and options were introduced.

But a cautious approach has been taken on derivatives on individual stocks, and the lucrative business was banished offshore to less regulated markets, where brokers are able to trade options or warrants based on Japanese stocks.

The Tokyo and Osaka exchanges will each list 20 stocks for option trading, including blue-chips such as Sony Corp and financials such as the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd. As seven of the stocks will be listed on both exchanges, only 33 stocks will be listed in total.
The launch will make Japan the third-largest stock option market in the world in terms of market capital, after the United States and Britain.

The options will be European-style with five strike prices for each expiry -- an at-the-money strike, two strike levels above and two below. There will be only four contract maturities, the most distant of which will be at most eight months out.
The contracts will be settled through the delivery of a number of stocks equal to the trading lots on the bourse. For most issues, one option contract will cover 1,000 shares.
Brokers expect that institutional investors will write covered calls against shares in their portfolios, in order to earn premiums on stocks at hand.

"Foreign investors and major brokerages will be able to use options to hedge positions, but it remains to be seen whether they will be able to use the tool successfully, considering costs," a trader at a second-tier brokerage said.
Despite such opportunities for hedging and earning premiums, there are still many wrinkles which need to be ironed out before options trade can flourish, market sources said.
They said Japanese investors were not widely familiar with stock options and several tax issues need to be sorted out.
According to the Japan Securities Dealers' Association (JSDA), profits from option trading are to be treated as miscellaneous income under the Income Tax Law.
The JSDA has yet to decide, however, how taxes will be assessed when margin transactions are used at the time of settlement. A decision is due by mid-September, when the first contract matures.

"The listing of options was decided on before issues such as taxes on margin trade were decided," a dealer at a medium-sized brokerage said. "The settlement process is confusing enough as it is, and the back offices will be in an uproar once trades start."
Richard May, research analyst at D.E. Shaw Securities Japan, added that with the most distant options contract only eight months out, investors may not find options attractive.

"The time span is short and it may be easy to predict what will happen eight months on," he said. "Investors may opt to stick to warrants and convertible bonds when it comes to derivatives, as they have much longer dates. The longer the time, the more things can happen."
Some worried that the sudden increase in trading instruments could create new complications for risk management.
"The back office will become extremely busy once options start and we cannot rule out the possibility of trouble with customers," a broker at a medium-sized brokerage said.
